_readme: Content AISA has written to fill gaps in the published ADEK pack.
The pack's lessons refer to printed artefacts a teacher hands out — a dataset card, a
criteria card — and to diagrams that exist as images in the PDF and so did not survive
text extraction. A student reading the lesson on screen is told to 'read the three lenses
on the criteria card' with no card in front of them.
These supplements fill those specific holes. They are kept separate from the extracted
lessons, and every section is marked authored:true so it renders with a note saying it is
AISA's addition and not ADEK material. Nothing here changes a worksheet task, a mark
scheme or a framework tag — only what a student reads.

section.label: How a data problem becomes an output mistake
section.heading: One flaw, traced all the way to the answer
section.altText: A chain of three boxes: a data problem leads to a wrong learned pattern, which leads to a wrong output.
section.caption: This is the chain you trace on your worksheet. Start at the data, not the answer.

section.label: Your dataset card
section.heading: What a dataset card shows you
section.intro: Your teacher gives you a card describing one dataset. Read it in this order — the flaw is never announced, you have to find it.

entries.asks: How many items are there, and what is each one a picture of?
entries.test: A small set is not automatically a bad one.

entries.asks: What is each example called? Is every label correct?
entries.test: One wrong label teaches one wrong lesson.

entries.asks: Does the set cover the real range of cases, or only some of them?
entries.test: A gap is as damaging as an error.

entries.asks: Is anything blurry, inconsistent or irrelevant?
entries.test: Noise makes the pattern harder to find.

section.label: The difference you are looking for
section.heading: Two ways a system can reach an answer
section.altText: Two columns. A rule-based system takes an input, follows a rule a person wrote, and gives an output. A learning system takes labelled examples, finds a pattern itself, and uses that pattern on a new input.
section.caption: Both give an answer. The difference is **where the rule came from** — a person wrote it, or the system found it.

left.title: Rule-based system
steps: Follow the rule a person wrote

right.title: Learning system
steps: Use it on a new input

section.label: Criteria card
section.heading: The three lenses
section.intro: Judge your solution through each lens in turn. A solution can be accurate and still fail the other two.

entries.asks: How often does it give the right or sensible answer?
entries.test: Test it with examples where you already know the correct answer, and record the score.

entries.asks: Does it actually help your user do their task?
entries.test: Check it against the real task you designed it for, not a task that happens to suit it.

entries.asks: What could go wrong, and who could be harmed?
entries.test: Check for unfair results and for any private data being exposed.
